newsitem.title: TAIWAN: Taiwan blocks air protest over Japan-held isles.
newsitem.headline: Taiwan blocks air protest over Japan-held isles.

text.p: Taiwan said on Thursday it had denied approval to local activists who had hoped to fly over a disputed East China Sea archipelago in the latest challenge to Japan's claim of sovereignty.

A multi-agency task force "recommended that the government not allow Protect-the-Diaoyus people to rent helicopters to go to the Diaoyu islands based on the national interest and the people's safety", vice foreign minister Cheng Wen-hua said.

The activists had hoped to mark the 51st anniversary of Taiwan's 1945 return from a half-century of Japanese colonial rule on Friday by dropping flags on the deserted islands claimed by Japan as the Senkakus and Taiwan and China as the Diaoyus.

Seeking to placate disappointment over the scuttled protest and appease anger over recent Japanese moves to assert sovereignty, the government task force said it would recommend that Taipei press Tokyo for further negotiations on the issue.

"We will ask the Japanese government and the Japanese people to exercise self-restraint to avoid escalation of the matter," Cheng said. "Our compatriots should also face this situation with a clear mind."
Taiwan wanted to resolve the dispute through "peaceful and rational means", he added.
State-funded television said the Civil Aeronautics Administration had informed local airlines not to rent helicopters to the activists.
Two rounds of Japan-Taiwan talks, unofficial due to their lack of diplomatic ties, have failed to defuse the situation. Japan recognises only the Beijing government, Taiwan's rival.
Foreign minister John Chang said on Wednesday that Taipei and Tokyo would hold a third round of talks on fishing rights and other issues stemming from the sovereignty row in Taipei.
He gave no exact date for the next round of talks.

On October 7, Taiwan and Hong Kong activists broke through a Japanese maritime cordon and hoisted flags of Taiwan's exiled Republic of China and the arch rival communist People's Republic of China on the islands.
Tokyo voiced regret for what it called the illegal landing and vowed to take necessary measures to stop similar actions.

Japanese rightists have triggered an angry and increasingly nationalistic backlash from ethnic Chinese across Asia after raising Japan's flag and building a lighthouse on the islands in July to assert Tokyo's claim.
Taiwan fishermen complain that Japanese patrol boats have barred them from fishing waters near the islands.
Japanese patrols also repulsed earlier attempts to land Taiwan and Hong Kong protesters on the islands, deepening anti-Japanese resentment in Taiwan, Hong Kong, Macau and the communist mainland.
Japan took the islands as war booty after defeating imperial China in 1895 and refuses to acknowledge that the dispute is open for discussion with China or Taiwan.
China and Taiwan say the islands have been Chinese territory for centuries and should have been returned after Japan's defeat in World War Two.
